newsitem.title: FRANCE: French insurer GAN reports big 96 loss.
newsitem.headline: French insurer GAN reports big 96 loss.

text.p: French State-controlled insurer Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN) revealed a 1996 loss of 5.68 billion francs ($973.5 million) on Monday as it sought to put huge losses in the property business behind it and prepare for privatisation.

The company, which is 80 percent-controlled by the state and has been promised a government aid package of 20 billion francs to try to get it ready for sale to the private sector this year, made a net attributable loss of 5.683 billion francs in 1996.

This compared to a 1995 loss of 1.786 billion francs and was mainly due to losses of 5.3 billion francs from property banking after an audit re-evaluating exposure to bad loans and the costs of dealing with its troubles since the property market collapsed at the end of the 1980s.

The loss is part of a clean-up after what Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has described as a "grim misadventure" of strategic error and mismanagement, but also an "optimistic" assessment of the group's situation by state administrators and regulators.

GAN said in its results statement that profits from its life insurance activities in France came to 825 million francs last year, compared to 451 million in 1995. Life assurance sales increased 9.9 percent to 25.2 billion francs.

Traditional life assurance business sales rose two percent but the lucrative Socapi joint venture with GAN's banking unit Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC) -- which is slated for privatisation before its parent -- saw sales rise 23 percent and generated 354 million francs out of total life assurance profit.
Non-life insurance sales fell 1.6 percent to 14.3 billion.

But the loss narrowed to 112 million francs from 567 million a year earlier, with a small profit registered in the second six months of 1996 as the group cut operating costs and improved the ratio of claims versus premiums, GAN's statement said.

Profit fell in the international insurance division to 321 million francs from 496 million. The group said this followed the sale in 1996 of GAN Belgium, HNL in the United States, Elite in Canada and the reinsurer CTR.
But exceptional charges of 1.365 billion francs dragged the combined result from the three life assurance divisions to a loss of 331 million francs for the year.
The big hole in the accounts came from UIC, which -- after the audit that led to the state rescue plan -- racked up a loss of 7.985 billion francs, versus 1.849 billion francs in 1995.

The governent announced plans in February to provide a state capital injection of 11 billion francs this year, seven billion to shore up the accounts of what Arthuis called the "diseased" UIC property banking arm, and 3.9 billion on the insurance side.
It has promised to cover bad loans to property developers and the sell-off of property assets and estimated the cost of that at a further nine billion francs.

Arthuis said when unveiling the rescue on February 27 that he hoped to isolate the insurance and CIC banking divisions with a view to privatisation "during the course of 1997" but still has to get the go-ahead from the European Commission, which vets state aid to firms in the European Union and already cleared a 2.8 billion-franc government aid package last year.

The government has already tried once to privatise the CIC grouping of regional banks but called off the trade sale tender last year after getting just two offers, from French banks BNP and Societe Generale , of which only the latter was ruled eligible by France's Privatisation Commission. ($ = 5.834 French Francs)
